notes: Complete EWCA Civ judgment on IAT review of Article 8 proportionality where adjudicator and SSHD differed on facts.

enrichment.short_title: IAT entitled to overturn adjudicator on Article 8 proportionality where age, military service and lack of home did not make removal disproportionate
key_facts: Mr Vujnovic, a Bosnian national of Serb origin, claimed asylum in the UK in September 2001 citing persecution and Articles 3, 8 and 14 ECHR.

An adjudicator upheld refusal under the Refugee Convention and Article 3 but allowed the appeal on Article 8, finding family life with his mother, brother and fiancée and that removal to Bosnia would be disproportionate.

The Immigration Appeal Tribunal reversed the adjudicator on proportionality; the Court of Appeal held the IAT was entitled to do so because the appellant's age (27), liability to military service and lack of a home in Croatia or Bosnia were not relevant factors weighing against removal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal with permission of Sedley LJ against the Immigration Appeal Tribunal's decision on an Article 8 human rights appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; leave to appeal to the House of Lords refused.
enrichment.ratio: Where an adjudicator finds family life engaging Article 8 on facts different from those before the Secretary of State, the IAT may independently review proportionality; but factors such as the appellant's age, possible future military service and absence of a home abroad do not, without evidence of dependence, make removal a disproportionate interference with family life in the United Kingdom.
legal_issues: Scope of the IAT's powers when reviewing an adjudicator's proportionality decision under section 65 of the 1999 Act
Whether military service liability and lack of a home abroad are relevant to the Article 8 proportionality balance
Application of Edore, Razgar, Djali and Ala on deference to the Secretary of State on immigration control

notes: Complete Admin Court judgment on SFO disclosure of seized pharmaceutical documents to the Department of Health.

enrichment.short_title: SFO lawfully disclosed seized Warfarin documents to DoH but acted unfairly by giving inadequate time for representations
key_facts: Kent Pharmaceuticals challenged the SFO's decision to disclose copies of documents seized under search warrants in a penicillin and Warfarin price-fixing investigation to the Department of Health for civil recovery proceedings.
The court rejected challenges to the lawfulness of seizure of five sample documents and held section 3(5)(a) of the 1987 Act was sufficiently precise to satisfy Article 8(2) 'in accordance with law'.

The SFO failed to act fairly in January 2003 by disclosing documents the day after forewarning KP, and should notify owners after disclosure where advance notice is required; discretionary relief remained to be argued.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Claim for judicial review by Kent Pharmaceuticals of SFO disclosure decisions, following earlier unsuccessful challenge to the search warrants.
enrichment.outcome: Claim met with limited substantive success on fairness and post-disclosure notification grounds; relief to be determined on hand-down.
enrichment.ratio: Disclosure by the SFO to another government department under section 3(5)(a) of the Criminal Justice Act 1987 for use in civil litigation to recover public funds is 'in accordance with law' for Article 8 purposes, but where advance notice of intended disclosure is practicable the SFO must allow reasonable time for representations and, if advance notice is not given, notify the owner promptly afterwards so that access to court is not frustrated.
legal_issues: Whether five specified documents were lawfully seized under the warrant or PACE section 19
Whether section 3(5)(a) confers an insufficiently defined discretion incompatible with Article 8(2)
Fairness requirements before and after disclosure to a government department
Whether secrecy about disclosure engages Article 6 access to court

notes: Complete Commercial Court trial judgment dismissing forex trading claim against Bank of India Jersey branch.

enrichment.short_title: Bank entitled to close customer's matched yen positions after margin shortfall; alleged 10% margin deal not proved
key_facts: Mr Sharad Patel traded foreign exchange through the Bank of India's Jersey branch under standard margin and guarantee agreements with a US$20 million limit and 50% additional margin trigger.
In June 1998 the Bank closed Mr Patel's matched buy/sell yen positions after he refused further margin and sought instructions that would have exceeded his trading limit.

Mr Patel alleged the Bank had orally agreed to reduce the 50% trigger to 10%, wrongly forced covering trades, and closed positions without authority; Morison J found his evidence unreliable and dismissed all heads of claim.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of breach of contract and related claims in the Commercial Court after refusal of a Part 24 strike-out at the end of the claimant's case.
enrichment.ratio: Under the Bank's trading agreement clause 4(c), the Bank had an independent discretion to take protective market action where a customer held large trapped losses and would not provide margin or trade within limits; the customer failed to prove any oral variation reducing the 50% margin requirement, and unauthorised trading and missing account claims were rejected.

Whether the Bank was entitled to refuse instructions of 25 June 1998 and close positions in July 1998

notes: Complete EWCA Civ judgment on hotel lease rent review proviso construction; majority dismissed appeal.

enrichment.short_title: Hotel lease rent-review proviso requiring best endeavours to maximise bedroom revenue is a formula assumption, not a damages covenant
key_facts: Burford, landlord of the Post House Hotel York, disputed whether proviso (1) to the definition of Net Bedroom Revenue in a 1972 lease created an independent covenant or only qualified the rent-review formula.
The lease tied reviewed rent to Net Bedroom Revenue every fourteen years; the parties had agreed rent for 1999-2013 without adjusting for alleged failure to maximise bedroom income.

The deputy judge and the Court of Appeal (Arden and Auld LJJ; Chadwick LJ dissenting on mechanism) held proviso (1) adjusts gross receipts on the hypothesis of best endeavours rather than giving a separate damages claim.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission against a declaration on a preliminary issue tried in the Chancery Division.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; claim dismissed with costs.
enrichment.ratio: Proviso (1) to paragraph 1(e) of schedule 3 is a mandatory assumption for calculating Net Bedroom Revenue—'received' means receivable on the footing that the tenant used best endeavours to maximise bedroom revenue—rather than a freestanding covenant remediable in damages or enforceable through re-entry; the rent-review machinery, including arbitration under paragraph 7, provides the exclusive remedy for non-compliance.
legal_issues: Whether proviso (1) is a covenant, condition or provision within clauses 3-6 of the lease
Whether breach gives rise to damages or only adjusts NBR in the review formula
Whether 'received' can be read as 'receivable' including notional receipts
Effect of clause 3(31) information covenant and surveyor arbitration

notes: Complete Sullivan J judgment declaring 1997 planning permission did not authorise ship dismantling at TERRC Hartlepool.

enrichment.short_title: 1997 planning permission for dismantling redundant marine structures did not include dismantling ships at Able UK TERRC site

statutes_considered.title: Town and Country Planning (Assessment of Environmental Effects) Regulations 1988
Town and Country Planning (Environmental Assessment) (England and Wales) Regulations 1999

key_facts: Able UK sought to dismantle US National Defence Reserve Fleet ships at its TERRC site Hartlepool relying on a 1997 permission for dismantling/refurbishment of redundant marine structures.
The council's officer letter of 30 September 2003 stated dismantling ships was permitted; local residents challenged that view by judicial review.

Sullivan J held that in ordinary language and in context—including the incorporated Environmental Statement—'marine structures' did not include ships, which were referred to separately and whose dismantling was never environmentally assessed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of an informal officer's view on the scope of existing planning permission, with interim injunction restricting dismantling work.
enrichment.outcome: Judicial review granted; declaration that 'marine structures' in the 1997 permission does not include ships; interim restriction continued.
enrichment.ratio: Where a planning permission and incorporated Environmental Statement expressly distinguish 'marine structures' from 'ships', 'vessels' and 'merchant shipping', and describe only offshore modules and related activities, the permission cannot be read as authorising ship dismantling merely because ships are not expressly excluded; an Environmental Statement must describe proposed activities and their environmental effects, and silence on ship-breaking indicates it is not permitted.
legal_issues: Construction of 'marine structures' in the 1997 permission and incorporated documents
Application of Shepway principles on use of Environmental Statements to define permission
Whether officer's letter was a reviewable decision
Relationship with waste management licence conditions

statutes_considered.title: Housing Grants, Construction and Regeneration Act 1996

key_facts: London and Amsterdam Properties claimed £659,346 plus interest from Waterman Partnership for late release of steelwork design information on the Milton Keynes Mid-Summer Place project.

notes: Complete Chancery judgment finding solicitor negligent for failure to renew Passport Agency child registration after abduction.

enrichment.short_title: Solicitors liable for failing to renew Passport Agency inhibition after father abducted twins to Tunisia on renewed UK passport
key_facts: Pamela Hamilton Jones instructed David & Snape in February 1994 after her estranged husband Ridha Bougossa began Children Act proceedings; the firm obtained prohibited steps orders and registered the three children with the UK Passport Agency for twelve months.

The Agency's letter of 28 February 1994 stated registration would lapse after twelve months unless renewed; the firm did not re-register or advise renewal in 1995-1996 despite knowing Bougossa had obtained British naturalisation.
In July 1996 Bougossa added the twins to his UK passport and removed them to Tunisia; Neuberger J held the negligence caused the abduction and awarded £55,260 including £20,000 for mental distress.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court trial of professional negligence claim in contract and tort relating to Children Act proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Claim succeeded; judgment for £55,260 including interest from 1 January 2000.
enrichment.ratio: Solicitors acting for an obsessively concerned parent in Children Act proceedings owed a duty at least to advise on renewing Passport Agency registration before expiry where they had initiated registration and knew the father could obtain a British passport; breach caused the abduction via the UK passport route, and damages for mental distress are recoverable in contract where protecting the client's peace of mind and custody of her children was a major object of the retainer, applying Watts v Morrow and Farley v Skinner.
legal_issues: Scope of retainer and legal aid certificate
Causation between non-renewal and abduction via UK passport
Recoverability of mental distress damages despite F v Wirral
Quantum of general and special damages and Parry v Cleaver on third-party payments

notes: Complete Commercial Court judgment on setting aside service out for cobalt contract dispute.

enrichment.short_title: Permission to serve cobalt sale contracts in Japan not set aside for non-disclosure on CPR 6.20 application
key_facts: MRG (Japan) Ltd sued Engelhard Metals Japan Ltd in England for non-performance of four cobalt supply contracts governed by English law with exclusive English jurisdiction clauses.
David Steel J granted permission to serve out under CPR 6.20(5)(c)-(d); Engelhard applied to set aside for alleged non-disclosure of Kanto fraud background and delay.
Morison J held the without-notice application required disclosure only of matters relevant to jurisdiction, serious issue and forum conveniens—not full merits defences—and dismissed the application.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application to set aside an without-notice order granting permission to serve a claim form out of the jurisdiction.
enrichment.ratio: On an without-notice application for permission to serve out under CPR 6.20, full and frank disclosure extends only to facts material to whether there is a good arguable case within the rule, a serious issue to be tried and that England is clearly the appropriate forum; known potential merits defences, including alleged fiduciary breach and fraud context, need not be disclosed unless they could reasonably affect those jurisdictional questions.
legal_issues: Scope of full and frank disclosure on service-out applications
Whether Kanto fraud background and delay were material non-disclosure

notes: Complex body-release dispute with provisional domicile findings only; source judges metadata lists Hale but judgment delivered by Gibbs J.

enrichment.short_title: Deceased's body to be released to first wife not second wife after domicile and marriage validity dispute
key_facts: Imadul Haqq died in September 2003; his first wife Jannat (claimant) and second wife Alfia (by a September 2002 ceremony in Bangladesh) each sought release of his remains from the coroner.
The coroner refused both requests pending resolution; the court proceeded on agreed basis of provisional assessment without conclusive findings on domicile or Bangladeshi marriage validity.

Gibbs J declared the claimant entitled to the body, finding the weight of evidence favoured English domicile at death, so the first marriage subsisted and the second marriage would be void under English law.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Expedited judicial review converted into declaratory resolution of competing claims to release of the deceased's body for burial.
enrichment.outcome: Declaration that the claimant is the person entitled to release of the deceased's body; leave to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: Where competing claims to a body turn on lawful marriage and entitlement to administration, the person first entitled to letters of administration is ordinarily entitled to determine disposal; on the provisional evidence the deceased remained domiciled in England and Wales so the claimant remained his lawful wife, and practical Islamic burial considerations favoured prompt release to her rather than transfer to Bangladesh.

notes: Complete EWCA Civ boundary dispute on construction of September 1998 paddock transfer plan.

enrichment.short_title: Paddock boundary fixed by 61-metre measurement on transfer plan; extrinsic evidence inadmissible
key_facts: Mr and Mrs Horn and Mr and Mrs Phillips disputed the boundary between paddocks at Ghyll View and Lane End, York, after a series of transfers from a common vendor.
The critical transfer to the Horns on 1 September 1998 defined their paddock as land edged red with a southern boundary '61 metres or thereabouts'.

The recorder held a straight-line extension of the garden boundary applied; the Court of Appeal held the plan was not ambiguous, extrinsic evidence was inadmissible, and the Horns received exactly 61 metres.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission from a county court trial on boundary construction between neighbouring freeholders.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; boundary runs to the 61-metre mark; costs below from 21 days after 25 October 2002 ordered against claimants.
enrichment.ratio: Extrinsic evidence is admissible to construe a transfer only if the document is uncertain, contradictory or ambiguous; a precise 61-metre measurement with identifiable endpoints on the plan is not rendered ambiguous by an incidental continuation line between the houses, and courts should not strain to find ambiguity in title documents relied on by subsequent purchasers.
legal_issues: Whether the September 1998 transfer plan was ambiguous
Admissibility of extrinsic and surveyor evidence
Effect of 'or thereabouts' on measured boundary
Costs consequences of Part 36 offers in boundary litigation
